newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia ACCC to mull Wallis inquiry results.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia ACCC to mull Wallis inquiry results.

text.p: Monopolies watchdog, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC), said on Sunday the Wallis inquiry into the finance industry would be a factor in clearing mergers between Australia's largest banks.

"If Wallis did things to free up competition then that would certainly be a relevant factor in our analysis of competition," ACCC chairman, Allan Fels, said in an interview on Seven Network's Face to Face television program.
Australia's conservative coalition promised the finance sector inquiry in the run up to the federal election, which it won in a landslide in March this year.

A major issue of the inquiry, headed by businessman Stan Wallis, is to address whether mergers should be allowed between the big four banks: the National Australia Bank Ltd, Westpac Banking Corp, Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd and the Commonwealth Bank of Australia Ltd.
Fels said there were lots of competition issues facing the financial sector that were likely be addressed by the inquiry.

These included restrictions on foreign ownership, shareholding restrictions, the treasurer's policy of restricting mergers between the big six banks as well as questions of access to the payments system and prudential regulation.
"It doesn't mean that we would go along with big bank or other mergers but obviously when we assess competition, the freer it is the better the prospects for bank mergers," he said.
Fels said the ACCC had previously stated it believed there should be one strong regional bank operating in each Australian state.
A move by any of the big four banks to take over any of the regional banks at this time would be looked at very closely by the ACCC, Fels said.
He said an important factor for the ACCC in analysing mergers between Australia's four biggest banks was whether it would lead to higher prices through reduced competition.

"If there are four big players it is a little bit harder for any one of them to increase their rates if they have to worry about three plus a fringe than, say, if there is two big players only and they don't have to worry about a whole lot of other competitors," Fels said.
The Wallis inquiry is due to conclude by March next year with a draft report ready this month.
